passage: In the school hall, when the principal announced Sumit as winner of the science fair, applause filled the room. He looked for Urmila in the third row, his old project partner from Class 8, and found her clapping without looking at him. Later, at the display tables, she left as he approached. He felt a prickle of hurt. When he thanked the judges, he said, "Urmila's idea about the water sensor is why it works." The next day, he waited by the library door and said once, "I didn't want this to come between us. If you want to talk, I'm around." Urmila nodded slowly and said, "Maybe. Give me time." He didn't push, and walked to class.

qa.q: Which project idea did Sumit credit to Urmila?
What was Sumit feeling when Urmila left as he approached, and how did he respond?
qa.a: He felt hurt, but he stayed gracious. He shared credit with Urmila and reached out to her once instead of flaunting his win or pretending he did not care.

qa.q: What would you advise Sumit to do now?
qa.a: Give Urmila time, avoid flaunting the win, and stay friendly without pushing.

qa.q: How might Urmila see Sumit's win?
qa.a: Possibly with mixed feelings, such as pride in her own idea and pain at watching him win alone. She clapped without looking at him, but she also said "Maybe. Give me time."

grounding: The protagonist wins and a former friend turns cold; he is gracious, shares credit and reaches out once.

passage:
"Anirban! Wait up." Sachin jogged to catch him at the cycle stand.

Anirban didn't turn. "What."

"You've been off since the results. Is it the art prize?"

"Why would it be? You won. Congrats." He yanked his lock open.

"You helped me, though. That idea to paint the market from above, that was yours, from when we sketched on your terrace. I said so at assembly."

"Everyone heard you say 'thank you to my friends.' Plural."

Sachin winced. "Yeah. I should have said your name. I'm sorry."

Anirban finally looked at him. "It's not just that. We both entered. You got a certificate on stage. I got nothing."

"I know. I'm not going to go on about it. And I'm not pretending I don't care, either. I was really happy." Sachin paused. "If you want to sketch this Sunday, I'll be at the terrace. If not, that's okay."

Anirban shrugged and cycled off.

qa.q: Where did Anirban and Sachin sketch together?
qa.a: They sketched together on Anirban's terrace.

qa.q: What might Anirban be feeling after the art prize?
qa.a: Anirban seems hurt and envious, since both entered and only Sachin was praised, and he felt left out by the vague thanks at assembly.

qa.q: Which choices by Sachin were wise, and why?
qa.a: Sachin shared credit for the idea, apologised for not naming Anirban, and reached out once without pushing, which respected Anirban's feelings.

qa.q: If you were Anirban, what would you want from Sachin now?
qa.a: You might want some time to get over the loss, and to know the Sunday invitation is still real without being pressured into it.

grounding: It shows a teen who won while a former friend turns cold, staying gracious, sharing credit and reaching out once without flaunting or pretending not to care.

passage:
The day I got the state essay prize, Nandini stopped waiting for me after school. I'm Dilnaz, and we had written our entries side by side in the reading room, sharing one pencil sharpener and a lot of complaints.

At first I thought she was just busy. Then I saw her looking away when my name was read in assembly, and I understood. She had wanted it as much as I did.

I felt two things at once: proud and guilty. My aunt wanted me to post the certificate everywhere. I didn't. I also didn't say "it's nothing," because it wasn't, and Nandini would have known I was lying.

I wrote her one message: "I miss walking home with you. Your essay made me rewrite my ending, you know. If you ever want to swap drafts again, I'm here." She didn't reply for a week. Then she left a new draft on my desk, no note.

qa.q: What did Nandini leave on Dilnaz's desk?
qa.a: Nandini left a new draft on Dilnaz's desk, with no note.

qa.q: What two feelings did Dilnaz have after the prize?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt proud of winning and guilty that the win had hurt Nandini, who had wanted the prize just as much.

qa.q: Why was it wise for Dilnaz not to post the certificate everywhere?
qa.a: Flaunting the win would have deepened Nandini's hurt, while staying quiet let Dilnaz reach out without rubbing it in. 🙂

qa.q: How might Nandini see the message Dilnaz sent?
qa.a: Nandini may have felt seen and credited, since Dilnaz admitted her essay shaped the ending, which could explain the draft she finally left.

grounding: It shows a teen whose win makes a friend turn cold, staying gracious, crediting the friend and reaching out once.
